questions.stem: A 20-year-old man presented with fever, rigors, neck pain, and respiratory distress. He had had a sore throat for the preceding week. On examination, his heart rate was 148 beats/minute, temperature 38.5°C, blood pressure 82/54 mmHg, SaO2 89% on room air. Examination of the oropharynx showed erythema over the soft palate and swollen tonsils. His neck movements were restricted, and there was tenderness and induration over the right jugular vein. Investigations: Peripheral white cell count 28.7 ×109/L (4.0–11.0) Platelets 67 ×109/L (150–400) CXR: multifocal bilateral infiltrates CT neck:
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: Fusobacterium necrophorum Lemierre’s syndrome is characterized by thrombosis and suppurative thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein. It is associated with disseminated septic emboli to the lungs and other sites. The most common pathogen is Fusobacterium necrophorum, but other organisms implicated include Eikenella, Bacteroides, and streptococcal species. Organisms may be isolated from blood cultures and from infective metastases. (Image from Assessments. In Cohen J, Powderly W , Opal S, eds. Infectious Diseases. 4th ed. Elsevier; 2017.)

questions.question: A 14-year-old female, healthy with no allergies, has 1 week of sore throat, non-productive cough, chest pain, dyspnea, and a unilateral exudative tonsil. Chest radiograph shows bilateral consolidation. Blood cultures grow pleomorphic gram-negative bacilli only in the anaerobic bottle.

questions.model_answer: a) Lemierre syndrome (septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein with septic pulmonary emboli). b) Fusobacterium necrophorum. c) Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck; expected finding is internal jugular vein thrombosis/thrombophlebitis. d) CT of the chest to evaluate the septic pulmonary emboli and detect empyema (feared complication; emboli may cavitate or cause empyema). e) A beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor such as piperacillin-tazobactam (F. necrophorum is often penicillin resistant), providing anaerobic and aerobic coverage.

questions.model_answer: a) Lemierre syndrome (jugular vein septic thrombophlebitis with septic pulmonary emboli). b) Fusobacterium necrophorum. c) Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck; expected to show internal jugular vein thrombosis. d) CT of the chest; expected to show cavitating septic pulmonary emboli and/or empyema. e) Piperacillin-tazobactam (or a beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor); metronidazole plus a beta-lactam/third-generation cephalosporin is an alternative, with 4-6 weeks of therapy.

questions.model_answer: a) Lemierre syndrome (internal jugular vein septic thrombophlebitis with septic pulmonary emboli). b) Fusobacterium necrophorum. c) Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck; expected to show internal jugular vein thrombosis. d) Blood cultures (bacteremia is universally present) and CT chest for septic emboli/empyema. e) Piperacillin-tazobactam, or ceftriaxone plus metronidazole, for 4-6 weeks; anticoagulation remains controversial with limited evidence.

cohort_answer.text: a) Lemierre's syndrome. b) Fusobacterium necrophorum. c) CTA of neck - demonstrating IJV thrombophlebitis. d) Blood cultures. e) Piperacillin-tazobactam (in case beta lactamase) OR CTX + Metronidazole; +/- anticoagulation.
